title: Would You Still Marry Them If the Money Disappeared Tomorrow?
paragraphs:
Would You Still Marry Them If the Money Disappeared Tomorrow?
The Question That Reveals Whether Your Heart Is Chasing God's Will... or Simply Looking for a Safer Life
What if everything they owned vanished overnight?
Would you still walk down that aisle?
That question is uncomfortable because it reaches far deeper than romance. It reaches into the hidden motives of the human heart.
Some are afraid of the answer.

We live in a world where financial stability has quietly become one of the greatest idols disguised as wisdom. Parents encourage it. Friends applaud it. Social media celebrates it. Society often calls it "being practical."
But Scripture asks a different question.

"The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance..."
(Proverbs 21:5)
The problem begins when money quietly replaces trust in God.
When financial security becomes the foundation of choosing a spouse instead of faith, character, holiness, covenant, and Christ.
There is an ancient Hebrew word that beautifully captures what God desires in marriage.
There is no single English word that fully translates it.
Loyal love that refuses to abandon someone when circumstances change.
Throughout the Old Testament, chesed describes God's own covenant love toward His people.
God compares His love—not to wealth—not to comfort—not to success—but to covenant faithfulness.
Marriage was designed to reflect that very love.
When Jesus affirmed marriage, He pointed people back to creation itself.

"So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
(Matthew 19:6)
The Greek word translated "joined together" is συνέζευξεν (synezeuxen).
God Himself is the One performing the joining.
That doesn't mean finances don't matter.
The Bible repeatedly teaches responsible stewardship.

"The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is slave to the lender."
(Proverbs 22:7)
Ignoring finances is not biblical wisdom.
Providing for one's family is commanded.

"If anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever."
(1 Timothy 5:8)
He says believers must become faithful providers.
The other focuses on becoming faithful.
The Bible gives us a breathtaking example in Ruth.
She became a poor foreign widow.
In human eyes, she had nothing to offer.
Yet Boaz did not marry Ruth because she could increase his wealth.
He married her because of her godly character.

"All my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman."
(Ruth 3:11)
The Hebrew expression is אֵשֶׁת חַיִל (eshet chayil).
It means a woman of noble character.
Likewise, Ruth never pursued Boaz merely because he was wealthy.
She sought redemption under God's covenant.
Their story ultimately points beyond themselves to Jesus Christ—the true Redeemer.
Even their marriage becomes part of the genealogy leading to Christ (Matthew 1).
What looked like scandal became grace.
A young woman marries a successful businessman.
If love depended upon financial security, the marriage begins to crumble.
But if the marriage rested upon Christ...
This is exactly what Jesus taught.

"Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock."
(Matthew 7:24)

"Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever."
(Hebrews 13:8)
That same chapter contains one of the strongest warnings regarding money.

"Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for He has said, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you.'"
(Hebrews 13:5)
The Greek phrase οὐ μή σε ἀνῶ οὐδ᾽ οὐ μή σε ἐγκαταλίπω (ou mē se anō oud' ou mē se enkataleipō) is one of the strongest possible expressions of negation in Koine Greek.
That is the security every human heart is actually searching for.
Does this mean it is always sinful to consider financial stability before marriage?
Biblical wisdom encourages asking honest questions.
Can this person manage money responsibly?
Do they honor God with their finances?
Will they lead our family in faithful stewardship?
But they are very different from asking,
One of the saddest realities today is that many people unknowingly marry financial security instead of a person.
And they discover they never truly loved the soul standing beside them.

"But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
(Romans 5:8)
Jesus did not wait until humanity became spiritually rich.
He came while we were spiritually bankrupt.
He loved us before we had anything to offer Him.
That is chesed fulfilled in Christ.
The cross forever destroys the idea that love is based upon personal gain.
So that grace could rewrite our story.
That is why Christian marriage is never ultimately about finding someone who makes life easier.
It is about two sinners transformed by Christ learning to display the Gospel together.
The greatest security in marriage has never been a salary.
It has always been the Savior.
Maybe this article has quietly exposed something inside your own heart.
Maybe you've been evaluating people through income instead of integrity.
Maybe you've been praying more for financial rescue than spiritual transformation.
Maybe you've realized that you've trusted money to give what only Jesus can provide.
The Gospel never ends in condemnation for those who come to Christ in repentance.
Because from the very beginning, God has specialized in rewriting impossible stories.

If this message challenged your heart, don't let it stop with you. Someone you love may be quietly wrestling with this very question. You never know how God may use one shared message to redirect a life toward biblical truth.
The safest place your heart will ever rest is not beside a wealthy spouse—but beneath the shadow of the cross.
